title: Vayikra: salt on every offering (Leviticus 2:13)
hook: "the salt of the covenant" on every offering, still sprinkled on bread today

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bowl of flour described with the word for soul. Your line was the poor bring their soul. Whose small gift did you honor? Day three hundred eighty-three.

On Friday night in Jewish homes that keep the custom, after the blessing over the challah, the person cutting the bread does one small thing before handing it around. They sprinkle a little salt on it, or dip the piece into salt. It takes two seconds. Kids sometimes fight over who gets the saltiest piece. But that pinch of salt goes all the way back to a single verse in this week's portion, and to an altar that stood in Jerusalem long ago.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT, THE CHALLAH.` → `A PINCH OF SALT.` → `BACK TO ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "And every meal-offering of thine shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meal-offering; with all thy offerings thou shalt offer salt." Every offering, salted. Just two verses earlier, the Torah forbids leaven and honey on the altar. No rising, no sweetening. But salt, always. Why salt? The text calls it the salt of the covenant, and elsewhere the Torah speaks of a covenant of salt, one that lasts forever. Salt doesn't rot. It preserves. Readers have heard in it a sign of something that keeps, the way salt keeps food from spoiling: a covenant of salt is a promise that doesn't go bad. Rashi says the covenant with salt goes back to creation: when God divided the waters, the lower waters, the seas, were promised a place on the altar, in the salt that comes from the sea, and in the water poured there on Sukkot. Other midrashim add that the lower waters wept at being sent far from God. The farthest waters get to come near. And the bread? The Talmud says that while the Temple stood, the altar brought atonement. Now that it's gone, a person's table does. Later authorities drew the line from there: if the table is like the altar, the bread on it gets salt, like every offering. A pinch of salt on Friday night is an altar remembered in a kitchen.
screen: `EVERY OFFERING, SALTED.` · `SALT DOESN'T ROT.` · `THE SEA'S PLACE ON THE ALTAR.` · `THE TABLE BECOMES THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `SALT OF THE COVENANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: salt your bread and remember. If you can, take a small piece of bread or a cracker and a pinch of salt. If not, just picture it. Sprinkle the salt slowly. As you do, think of one promise in your life that has kept: a friendship that didn't spoil, a commitment someone kept to you, one you've kept to someone else. Taste the salt, or imagine it. Let it stand for everything that lasts. Then breathe, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Vayikra. And He called. The book that commands salt on every offering: the salt of the covenant.
Your line: salt of the covenant. Today, at one meal, salt your food on purpose and remember a promise that kept. Day three hundred eighty-three.

what a scholar hears: Rashi on 2:13 cites the midrash of the lower waters promised salt and water on the altar; Berakhot 55a says a person's table now atones like the altar, the root of salting the bread.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'many Jewish homes', 'most people do it without thinking' and 'almost two thousand years'; salt as permanence framed as a reading; Rashi corrected (he gives the promise to the lower waters; the weeping is from other midrashim); the salt-on-bread link attributed to later authorities.
Leviticus 2:13 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
Rashi on 2:13 (the lower waters promised salt on the altar and the water libation of Sukkot): confirm.
Berakhot 55a (the table atones as the altar did) and the salting custom (e.g., Shulchan Aruch OC 167:5 and commentaries): confirm the link as stated.
Salt as a sign of permanence in the ancient Near East: stated generally; confirm.
'Almost two thousand years' since the Temple's destruction in 70 CE.
